Covers biology, identification, soils, and pruning
Includes tree risk, diagnosis, and safety
Review questions at the end of chapters
Useful reference long after the exam

p: The arborists' certification study guide walks through the knowledge areas the ISA exam tests: tree biology, identification and selection, soil management, installation and establishment, pruning, diagnosis and treatment, tree protection, urban forestry, tree risk management, and safe work practices. Each chapter ends with review questions so you can check what stuck.
Many people call it the ISA book or ISA study guide; it is the official text candidates are pointed to.

The guide is written for people with some field experience. If you have been working in tree care for a few years, much of the material will feel familiar, but chapters on soils, biology, and diagnosis often fill gaps that day-to-day work does not cover.

Read a chapter a week, take notes in your own words, and work through the review questions. Tie each chapter to something you see on the job. Pair the guide with the ANSI A300 standard and ANSI Z133, which the exam draws on. Check ISA's current exam requirements and edition before buying.

Set a test date a few months out and work backward to plan your reading. Study groups and practice exams help, and many local ISA chapters run review courses. Keep the guide after you pass; it is a solid reference for continuing education and for explaining recommendations to clients.

faq.q: Is the study guide enough to pass?
faq.a: Many candidates pass with the guide plus field experience. Practice tests and study groups help.

faq.q: Which edition should I buy?
faq.a: Buy the current edition ISA lists for the exam you plan to take.

name: Husqvarna 3/8 in x .050 Full Comp Chainsaw Chain
title: Husqvarna Chainsaw Chain 3/8 x .050 Full Comp
h1: Husqvarna Chainsaw Chain, 3/8 in x .050 Full Comp
meta: Husqvarna chainsaw chain in 3/8 in pitch and .050 gauge with a full complement of cutters. How to match drive links, fit your bar, and typical price.
tagline: 3/8 in pitch, .050 gauge full-comp chain for mid-to-large Husqvarna saws.
summary: This Husqvarna chainsaw chain is 3/8 in pitch, .050 gauge, with a full complement of cutters for fast, smooth cutting. It fits mid-to-large saws running 3/8 in .050 bars and is a common choice for felling and bucking.
highlights: 3/8 in pitch for mid-to-large saws
Standard .050 gauge
Full complement cutters for smooth, fast cutting
Ready to run out of the box
Order by drive link count to match your bar

p: Saw chain has to match three numbers on your bar: pitch, gauge, and drive link count. This chain is 3/8 in pitch and .050 gauge. The drive link count depends on bar length and the bar's nose sprocket, and it is stamped on most bars near the mount. Order the link count shown there, not just the bar length, because two 20 in bars can take different chains.
3/8 in pitch is common on saws in the 60 cc and up range, as well as many 50-60 cc saws set up with longer bars. If your bar says .325 or .058, this is not the chain for it.

People searching for chainsaw chain for Husqvarna saws often assume the chain is saw-specific. It is not: the chain fits the bar, and the bar fits the saw. Any bar with the right pitch, gauge, and link count will take this chain.

Full-comp chain has a cutter on every tie strap position the pattern allows, so more teeth are in the wood at once. That gives smooth, fast cuts in the 16 to 24 in bar range most crews run. Skip chain, with fewer cutters, clears chips better on very long bars; for everyday felling, bucking, and storm work, full comp is the standard choice.
Running a spare loop or two on the truck means you can swap a dull chain in a couple of minutes and sharpen the old one later at the shop.

Husqvarna chains also come in different cutter styles. Chisel cutters cut fastest in clean wood; semi-chisel cutters hold an edge longer in dirty wood. Pick the style that matches how you work, and match it to the right file size when sharpening.
When you buy several loops at once, label each with its drive link count and the bar it fits. A mixed truck box of unmarked chains is a quick way to lose time on site.
Run a new chain at low load for a few minutes, then let it cool and recheck tension, since new chain stretches as it seats. Keep the bar oiler working and the oil reservoir full.

Sharpen with the file size and angle in Husqvarna's chart for this chain, take the same number of strokes on each cutter, and lower depth gauges every few sharpenings. Replace the chain when cutters are worn back to the wear marks or when links are cracked. Pair new chain with a fresh chain loop rotation and a sprocket check: a worn rim sprocket eats new chain quickly.
Always wear chainsaw-rated leg protection, gloves, eye and hearing protection, and a helmet when running a saw.

If the chain starts to cut crooked, check for uneven cutters or a worn bar rail before blaming the chain. Dress the bar rails with a flat file and flip the bar every time you change the chain so both rails wear evenly.

faq.q: How do I know which Husqvarna chain fits my saw?
faq.a: Read the pitch, gauge, and drive link count stamped on your bar, then match all three.

faq.q: Will this chain fit other brands of saw?
faq.a: It fits any bar made for 3/8 in pitch, .050 gauge chain with the matching drive link count, regardless of saw brand.

faq.q: Full comp or skip chain?
faq.a: Full comp for most bars up to about 24 in. Skip chain is common on long bars where chip clearance matters more.

name: Husqvarna 3/8 in x .063 Gauge Chainsaw Chain
title: Husqvarna Chainsaw Blade: 3/8 x .063 Chain for Big Bars
h1: Husqvarna 3/8 in x .063 Chainsaw Blade and Chain
meta: Need a chainsaw blade Husqvarna big saws can run on 28 to 36 in bars? This 3/8 in x .063 gauge chain suits large saws. Fit, sizing, and typical price.
tagline: Heavy .063 gauge chain for large saws and long bars.
summary: If you are shopping for a chainsaw blade Husqvarna big saws can pull on a long bar, this is it: 3/8 in pitch chain in heavy .063 gauge. It suits large-displacement saws and long bars, including 36 inch chainsaw bar and chain setups for big wood.
highlights: 3/8 in pitch, .063 gauge
For large saws and long bars
Available in long loops for 28 to 36 in bars
Heavier drive links stand up to big-wood work

p: Gauge is the thickness of the drive links where they ride in the bar groove. Most saws run .050 or .058, but many long bars for big saws use .063. This chain is for those bars, typically on 80 cc and larger saws used for felling and bucking large trees.
For a 36 inch chainsaw chain, match the drive link count stamped on your bar. A wrong count will not tension correctly, and the wrong gauge will either bind or wobble in the groove.

Long bars are common for felling large trees, bucking big rounds, and milling. A 36 in bar on a powerful saw lets you cut big stems from one side and reach through wide trunks, but it also demands a sharp, correctly matched chain to keep the saw pulling.

Keep the oiler set high and check that oil reaches the nose. File every cutter evenly, since a chain that pulls to one side on a 36 in bar wanders badly in the cut. Wear full chainsaw PPE and plan escape routes before felling. Browse more chainsaw chain for other sizes.
Check chain tension often, since long chain stretches more, and keep tension right when the chain is warm. Store long loops coiled in a sealed bag with a little bar oil to keep them from rusting.

faq.q: Will a .063 chain fit a .050 bar?
faq.a: No. The drive links are too thick for a .050 or .058 groove.

faq.q: Does this chain fit a 36 inch bar?
faq.a: Yes, in the loop length matching your bar's drive link count and 3/8 in .063 groove.

name: Husqvarna X-Cut SP33G Semi-Chisel Chain .325 x .050
title: Husqvarna X-Cut SP33G Chain .325 x .050 Semi-Chisel
h1: Husqvarna X-Cut SP33G Chain, .325 x .050 Semi-Chisel
meta: Husqvarna X-Cut SP33G chain is a .325 pitch, .050 gauge semi-chisel chain for 40 to 60 cc saws. Fitment, 20 in loops, sharpening tips, and price.
tagline: Low-vibration .325 semi-chisel chain for mid-size saws.
summary: Husqvarna X-Cut SP33G chain is a .325 pitch, .050 gauge semi-chisel chain built for mid-size saws in the 40 to 60 cc range. It is pre-stretched, holds an edge well in dirty wood, and is a common factory chain on Husqvarna's popular 50-class saws.
highlights: Pitch .325 in, gauge .050 in
Semi-chisel cutters hold an edge in dirty or frozen wood
Pre-stretched to reduce re-tensioning
Low-vibration design
Common on 16 to 20 in bars for mid-size saws

p: Full-chisel cutters have a sharp square corner that cuts fast in clean wood but dulls quickly when it hits dirt, bark grit, or frozen wood. Semi-chisel cutters have a rounded corner that gives up a little speed and lasts much longer between sharpenings. For storm work, firewood, and ground-level bucking where the bar inevitably touches dirt, the SP33G is a forgiving choice.
Husqvarna's X-Cut line is pre-stretched at the factory, so you spend less time stopping to retension a new chain during the first tank.

SP33G is also a good choice for crews where several people share saws. Semi-chisel is more forgiving of imperfect sharpening, so the chain still cuts well even if not everyone files to the same standard.

SP33G is .325 pitch and .050 gauge. That matches a lot of 45 to 60 cc saws, including many Husqvarna 450, 455, and 550-class saws, depending on how they are set up. The Husqvarna X-Cut SP33G 20 inch chainsaw chain is one of the most common loops; 16 and 18 in loops are also popular.
Do not order by bar length alone. Check the drive link count stamped on your bar and match it exactly. A chain one link off will not tension properly.

Many users searching for Husqvarna SP33G chain are replacing the chain that came on their saw. If so, the old chain or the bar stamp will tell you the drive link count. Write it on the saw's case or in your saw log so the next order is easy.

Keep a few spare loops on the truck. Swapping a dull chain for a sharp one takes a couple of minutes and gets the saw cutting at full speed again, which is safer and faster than pushing a dull chain through the cut.

Use the round file size Husqvarna specifies for SP33G, hold the file at the angle marked on the cutters, and keep the same stroke count on every tooth. A Husqvarna file guide makes it easier to keep depth gauges at the right height. Sharpen when the saw starts throwing dust instead of chips or needs to be pushed through the cut.

Replace the chain when cutters are worn to the wear marks or the chain has cracked or damaged links, and check the drive sprocket when you put on a new chain. Keep a few spare loops of chainsaw chain in the truck.
New chain stretches during the first few cuts. Run it lightly, let it cool, and retension before working hard. Keep the bar oiler full and check that oil is reaching the chain.
Keep a round file, flat file, depth gauge tool, and file guide in your saw kit so you can touch up the chain in the field between tanks of fuel.

faq.q: What saws use SP33G chain?
faq.a: Many mid-size saws with .325 pitch, .050 gauge bars, including popular Husqvarna 45 to 60 cc models. Check your bar markings.

faq.q: How many drive links for a 20 in bar?
faq.a: It varies by bar. Use the drive link count stamped on your bar.

faq.q: Is SP33G full chisel?
faq.a: No. It is semi-chisel, which trades a little speed for longer edge life in dirty wood.

name: Economy Apron-Style Chainsaw Chaps
title: Economy Apron Style Chainsaw Chaps for Ground Work
meta: Economy apron style chainsaw chaps buckle around the waist and cover the front of your legs. Who they suit, how to size them, and when to replace them.
tagline: Budget apron chaps for occasional saw users and ground crews.
summary: These economy apron style chainsaw chaps buckle around your waist and wrap the front of your legs with cut-resistant layers. They are an affordable choice for ground workers, homeowners, and crews who need spare chaps on the truck.
highlights: Apron design goes on and off quickly
Cut-resistant layers across the front of the legs
Adjustable waist and leg straps
Budget-friendly spare set for crews

p: Apron chaps wrap the front and sides of your legs and buckle at the waist and behind each leg. When a moving chain contacts the chaps, the inner fibers pull out and clog the drive sprocket to stop the chain. They go over your work pants in seconds, which makes them handy for ground workers who pick up a saw on and off through the day.
Check the label for the standard the chaps are tested to, such as ASTM F1897 or a UL listing, before relying on them.
Apron chaps suit occasional saw users and ground workers who move between tasks. Climbers and full-time fellers often prefer full-wrap chaps or chainsaw pants that protect the back of the calf too.

Chaps should cover from the waist to about 2 in below the boot top. Snug the straps so the chaps do not shift. Replace chaps after any cut that reaches the protective layers, and keep them clean of oil and fuel. Compare other chainsaw chaps for full-wrap styles.
Chaps are not a reason to take chances. Keep two hands on the saw, keep your stance stable, and keep the bar away from your legs.
Store chaps flat or hanging, out of sunlight, and inspect them for cuts and wear before each use. Fuel and oil can weaken the protective fibers over time.

faq.q: Are apron chaps as safe as full-wrap chaps?
faq.a: They protect the front of the legs, where most cuts happen. Full-wrap chaps add calf protection.

faq.q: Can I wash chainsaw chaps?
faq.a: Follow the label. Many can be hand washed; harsh detergents and heat can reduce protection.

name: Bungee Chainsaw Lanyard with Snap
title: Bungee Lanyard for Chainsaws, with Snap
h1: Bungee Lanyard for Chainsaws, with Snap
meta: A bungee lanyard with snap keeps your chainsaw tethered to your saddle in the tree, stretching as you cut. How climbers use it and what to check before use.
tagline: Stretchy saw tether that keeps a top-handle saw on your saddle.
summary: This bungee lanyard tethers your chainsaw to your saddle so it stays with you when you let go. The bungee stretches as you cut and pulls back out of the way when you hang the saw.
highlights: Bungee stretches as you reach and cut
Snap end clips to the saw's lanyard ring
Keeps the saw from dropping
Tidy recoil reduces snagging

p: Dropping a saw from a tree is dangerous to your ground crew and expensive. A bungee lanyard keeps the saw attached while giving you room to reach. It recoils when you hang the saw so it does not dangle near your climbing line.
Clip the snap to the saw's lanyard ring and the other end to a tool loop or saw ring on your saddle.

A good saw lanyard is one of the cheapest pieces of protection in a climber's kit. It protects the crew below, the landscape, and the customer's property, and it keeps your expensive top-handle saw from hitting the ground.
Set it up so the saw hangs on your side away from your climbing system and does not tangle with your lanyard when you reposition.
Check the bungee for cuts and lost stretch, and make sure the snap closes fully. A chainsaw lanyard is not life-support equipment; never clip into it for positioning. See other chainsaw lanyards.
Retire the lanyard if the bungee is frayed or soft, or the snap does not close and lock fully. Keep it out of fuel and oil.
Check the attachment point on your saddle, too. A worn tool loop can let go just as easily as a worn lanyard.

faq.q: Can I use a bungee lanyard as a climbing lanyard?
faq.a: No. It is a tool tether only and is not rated for life support.

faq.q: How long should it be?
faq.a: Long enough to reach comfortably when stretched, short enough that the saw hangs clear of your feet and rope.

name: Weaver Bungee Modular Chainsaw Lanyard System
title: Weaver Leather Bungee Chain Strap: Modular Saw Lanyard
h1: Weaver Leather Bungee Chain Strap: Modular Chainsaw Lanyard
meta: Weaver's bungee modular chainsaw lanyard system, often searched as the Weaver Leather bungee chain strap, tethers a saw to your saddle. Setup and checks.
tagline: Modular bungee saw tether from Weaver for climbers.
summary: The Weaver bungee modular chainsaw lanyard system, often searched as the Weaver Leather bungee chain strap, keeps your saw tethered to your saddle while you work. The modular design lets you set it up to suit how you carry and hang your saw.
highlights: Bungee section stretches with your reach
Modular setup to suit your saddle
Weaver build quality
Keeps saws and tools from dropping

p: Every climber hangs a saw a little differently. A modular lanyard lets you arrange the bungee and connectors to suit your saddle, your saw, and whether you work mostly pruning or removals. The bungee gives reach when you cut and pulls the saw back in when you let go, keeping it away from your feet and climbing line.
It also works for hand saws or other tools you want tethered while you climb.

Weaver Leather has made climbing saddles and tree gear for many years, and its lanyards are built to last through daily use on a saddle. The bungee is designed to hold up to repeated stretching, and the connectors are sized to fit common saw rings.

Inspect the bungee for cuts or lost stretch and check every connector closes fully. This is a tool tether only; never use it for positioning or fall protection. Pair it with a top-handle saw like the Husqvarna T542i XP, or see other chainsaw lanyards.
Replace the lanyard if the bungee loses its stretch or the cover is cut. Keep the saw hanging on the side away from your climbing line so it does not interfere when you move.
Inspect the stitching and hardware regularly, and keep it clean of bar oil and sap.

faq.q: Is the Weaver bungee lanyard rated for life support?
faq.a: No. It is designed to tether tools only.

faq.q: Does it fit any saw?
faq.a: It clips to a saw's lanyard ring or attachment point. Check the connector fits your saw.

name: Husqvarna 562XP Mark II Chainsaw
title: Husqvarna 562XP Mark II Chainsaw: Specs & Buying Guide
meta: The Husqvarna 562XP Mark II is a 59.8 cc pro chainsaw with AutoTune for felling and bucking. Specs, bar options, who it suits, and typical price.
tagline: Pro 60 cc-class saw for felling, bucking, and storm work.
summary: The Husqvarna 562XP Mark II is a professional 59.8 cc chainsaw that sits at the heart of many tree crews' saw lineups. It is light for its power, runs AutoTune to adjust itself to conditions, and handles felling, bucking, and storm cleanup with a bar in the 18 to 24 in range.
highlights: 59.8 cc X-Torq engine
AutoTune adjusts the carburetor automatically
Strong power-to-weight for a 60 cc-class saw
Runs 18 to 24 in bars for most work
Updated Mark II design for durability
specs: .325 in or 3/8 in, depending on setup

p: Most tree crews end up with three saws: a top-handle for the climber, a 50 cc saw for limbing, and a 60 cc saw for felling and bucking. The Husqvarna 562XP has been a favorite in that last slot because it is powerful enough for real wood and light enough to carry all day. The 562 XP Husqvarna Mark II update keeps the same idea with improvements to durability and handling.
It is the saw you grab to drop a spar, buck the trunk into rounds for the loader, and clear storm wood on a long day.

The 59.8 cc X-Torq engine is built for lower emissions and fuel use than older designs. AutoTune adjusts the carburetor for fuel, altitude, temperature, and air filter condition, so the saw keeps running right without a tune-up screwdriver.

Most users run an 18 or 20 in bar for all-round work and go to 24 in for larger trees. Husqvarna lists a range of approved bar and chain combinations; stick to those. A .325 pitch setup gives smooth, fast cutting on shorter bars, while 3/8 in pitch handles longer bars and bigger wood. Pair it with fresh 3/8 in chain or SP33G .325 chain to match your bar.

Mark II updates focused on making the saw more durable and easier to service, which matters for crews that run a saw every working day and want it to stay reliable. If you already run the original 562XP, the Mark II will feel familiar in your hands.

The 562XP is a professional saw. It suits arborists, loggers, and serious firewood cutters who run a saw most days. If you only cut a few times a year, a smaller saw is easier to handle and maintain. If you regularly fell large hardwoods, consider a 70 cc-class saw alongside it.
Expect a learning curve if you come from homeowner saws: it revs faster and has more chain speed, so good technique matters.

The saw is light for its class, which pays off when you carry it across a property, up a slope, or on long storm-cleanup days. Good balance with an 18 to 20 in bar makes it comfortable for both felling and limbing.

Use fresh fuel mixed at 50:1 with quality 2-stroke oil, or a pre-mixed fuel. Clean the air filter and check the spark plug regularly, and keep the cooling fins clear of sawdust. Sharpen the chain often and keep the bar dressed.
Wear chainsaw-rated chaps or pants, a helmet with face and hearing protection, gloves, and cut-resistant boots. Plan felling cuts and escape routes, and follow ANSI Z133 and your training.

Have the saw serviced by a qualified dealer when it needs more than routine care. Inspect the chain brake, chain catcher, and throttle lockout before every use, and do not run the saw if any of them is damaged.

faq.q: What is the displacement of the Husqvarna 562XP?
What bar length should I run on a 562XP Mark II?
faq.a: Most users run 18 to 20 in for all-round work and up to 24 in for bigger trees. Use bar and chain combinations Husqvarna approves.

faq.q: What changed with the Mark II?
faq.a: The Mark II is an updated version of the 562XP with refinements to durability and handling while keeping the same engine size.

name: Replacement Pads for Gecko Climbers
title: Replacement Pads for Gecko Climbing Gear Spurs
h1: Gecko Climbing Gear Replacement Climber Pads
meta: Replacement pads for Gecko climbers restore comfort to worn spur cuffs. Learn when to swap pads, how to check fit, and what to inspect on Gecko climbing gear.
tagline: Fresh cuff pads to keep Gecko spurs comfortable on removals.
summary: These replacement pads fit Gecko climbers and restore comfort to the cuffs on your Gecko climbing gear. Fresh pads spread pressure across your calf so you can spike up removals without sore shins.
highlights: Made to fit Gecko climber cuffs
Restores padding that compresses with use
Spreads pressure across the lower leg
Cheaper than replacing the whole set

p: Spur pads flatten, crack, and soak up sweat and sap over a season. Once they stop cushioning, the cuff digs into your calf and you start adjusting your stance to avoid it, which makes climbing harder. A new set of pads brings the spurs back to how they felt when new.
Swap both sides at once so the fit stays even.

Comfort matters on spurs. When the cuffs fit well, you can stand on your gaffs with less fatigue and keep your attention on the cut rather than on your shins. That makes for a safer, more productive removal.
Gecko climbing gear users who climb in hot weather often find pads wear faster from sweat, so plan to replace them more often in summer.

With the pads off, check the shanks for cracks, the gaffs for length and sharpness, and the straps and buckles for wear. Spurs are for removals only; never spike a tree you are pruning. See more climber pads.
Clean and dry the pads after wet climbs to keep them from breaking down.
If the straps are worn or the buckles do not hold, replace them at the same time, since they work together with the pads to hold the spurs firmly in place. A loose spur is tiring and unsafe.

faq.q: Will these pads fit other spurs?
faq.a: They are made for Gecko climbers. Check fit before ordering for another brand.

faq.q: How often should I change pads?
faq.a: When they no longer cushion or are torn. Busy removal climbers may change them yearly.

name: Jameson Rope Sniper Rope Placement Tool
title: Jameson Rope Sniper Rope Placement Tool
h1: Jameson Rope Sniper Rope Placement Tool
meta: The Jameson Rope Sniper is a pole-mounted head for placing a rope or line over a limb from the ground. How it works, where it helps, and typical price.
tagline: Pole-mounted head for setting a line over a limb from the ground.
summary: The Jameson Rope Sniper is a pole-mounted rope placement tool that lets you set a line over a limb from the ground. It mounts on a Jameson pole and speeds up line placement on lower crotches where a throw bag is slow or awkward.
highlights: Mounts on a Jameson pole
Places line over limbs from the ground
Useful for low and mid-height crotches
Helps with re-sets and pull-lines

p: A throw bag is the go-to for high anchors, but low and mid-height crotches are often quicker with a pole. The Rope Sniper holds the line on the pole head so you can lift it over a limb and drop it in place, then pull the pole away. It is handy for setting pull-lines, re-setting a climbing line, and working in crowded crowns where throws keep snagging.
Reach is limited by your pole, so it complements a throw line kit rather than replacing it.

The tool is also useful for placing a line at the right spot over a union when you need to isolate a specific crotch. With a pole, you can see and control where the line lands more precisely than with a throw.
Ground crews also use pole tools to retrieve lines that hang up on a lower limb, saving the climber a trip.
Keep poles well clear of power lines; follow ANSI Z133 approach distances. Confirm your anchor before climbing. See more in climbing rope.
Before climbing on any anchor set from the ground, confirm the limb is alive, sound, and large enough for the load, and that the line went over the intended union.
Keep the pole sections clean so they lock and unlock smoothly, and store them out of the sun.

faq.q: Does the Rope Sniper fit other poles?
faq.a: It is designed for Jameson poles. Check the fitting before using another brand.

faq.q: Can it replace a throw bag?
faq.a: Not for high anchors. It is best for crotches within pole reach.

name: Petzl GriGri Belay Device
title: Petzl GriGri Belay Device: Specs, Uses & Price
meta: The Petzl GriGri is an assisted-braking belay device for 8.5 to 11 mm ropes. What it does, how it differs from the GriGri+, rope fit, and typical price.
tagline: Petzl's assisted-braking belay device for single ropes 8.5 to 11 mm.
summary: The Petzl GriGri is the best-known assisted-braking belay device, built to help a belayer catch and hold a fall on single ropes from 8.5 to 11 mm. It is compact, light, and simple, and it is the reference device many climbers learn on.
highlights: Assisted braking on single ropes 8.5 to 11 mm
Weighs about 175 g
Handle for controlled lowering
Works for lead and top-rope belaying
Simple, durable design

p: The GriGri belay device uses a cam that pinches the rope when it moves suddenly, as in a fall. The belayer still keeps a hand on the brake strand at all times, but the cam adds a backup if the belayer is distracted or hit by falling debris. To lower, the belayer pulls the handle while controlling speed with the brake hand.
The current Petzl GriGri covers ropes from 8.5 to 11 mm, so it fits the single ropes most climbers use in the gym and at the crag.
Its compact, light body makes it easy to carry on a harness, and the simple design is easy for new climbers to learn with qualified instruction.

The GriGri+ adds an anti-panic function that stops the descent if the belayer pulls the handle too hard, and a selector for top-rope or lead mode. Those features suit gyms, new belayers, and anyone who wants extra margin. The standard GriGri is lighter and simpler, and many experienced climbers prefer it for that.
Both share the same rope range and basic operation, so moving between them is easy.
Price is another difference. The standard GriGri usually costs less than the GriGri+, which matters if you are buying several devices for a gym or a training program.
If you are unsure which suits you, borrow both at the gym and try lowering a partner with each.

Tree climbers usually run 11 to 13 mm ropes and purpose-built devices for MRS and SRS. Rope diameter alone puts most arborist climbing lines outside the GriGri's range. Some crews use a GriGri in rescue or work-positioning setups with compatible rope, but that is outside its primary design.

The GriGri is designed and certified as a belay device for rock and gym climbing. If you plan to use it in a tree-work system, make sure the configuration is covered by Petzl's instructions, that it meets ANSI Z133 requirements for life support, and that you are trained in it. Inspect it before every use.

If your crew already climbs on smaller-diameter rope for rescue or rope access work, check that every part of your system, including the rope, carabiners, and anchors, is compatible and rated for the job.

Keep sand and grit out of the cam and rope channel, and rinse with clean water if it gets dirty. Check the cam moves freely and springs back, look for wear grooves where the rope runs, and retire the device if parts are cracked or deformed. Follow Petzl's inspection guidance and record checks for crew gear.

Keep the device away from solvents and chemicals that can damage the plastic side plate. Store it dry, away from heat. If it has been dropped from height or caught a severe fall, inspect it carefully and retire it if in any doubt.

faq.q: What rope diameter does the Petzl GriGri take?
faq.a: Single ropes from 8.5 to 11 mm.

faq.q: Is the GriGri hands-free?
faq.a: No. The belayer must always hold the brake strand. The cam is a backup, not a substitute.

faq.q: Can arborists use a GriGri for tree climbing?
faq.a: Most arborist climbing ropes are thicker than its range, and it is designed as a belay device. Use devices designed and approved for tree climbing systems.

name: Petzl GriGri+ Belay Device
title: Petzl GriGri+ Belay Device with Anti-Panic
meta: The Petzl GriGri+ is an assisted-braking belay device with anti-panic and a lead or top-rope mode selector. Rope range, key features, and typical price.
tagline: GriGri with anti-panic lowering and a lead/top-rope mode selector.
summary: The Petzl GriGri+ takes the familiar GriGri design and adds an anti-panic handle and a mode selector for top-rope or lead belaying. It handles single ropes from 8.5 to 11 mm and is a popular choice for gyms, teaching, and climbers who want extra margin when lowering.
highlights: Anti-panic handle stops descent if pulled too far
Selector for top-rope or lead mode
Single ropes 8.5 to 11 mm
Steel wear plate for durability
Weighs about 200 g

p: The anti-panic feature is the headline. If a belayer yanks the handle all the way open while lowering, the GriGri+ locks and stops the descent instead of letting the climber drop. Ease the handle back and lowering resumes. That catches one of the most common belay mistakes, especially with newer belayers.

The mode selector lets you set the device for top-rope or lead. In top-rope mode it engages more readily; in lead mode it pays out rope smoothly for clipping. A steel wear plate in the rope channel extends service life on gym ropes that see heavy use.
The GriGri+ is a little heavier than the standard GriGri because of the extra features. For most climbers, especially in gyms, the extra margin is worth the small weight difference.

Whichever version you use, the rule is the same: the brake hand never leaves the rope. The cam is a backup. Load the rope following the diagram on the device, test it with a sharp tug before every climb, and keep the handle under control on the lower.
Compare it with the standard Petzl GriGri if you want a lighter, simpler device and are confident in your lowering technique.
Lowering is where most belay accidents happen. Feed the rope smoothly and keep the climber's descent slow and steady. The anti-panic handle is a backup, not a substitute for good technique.
Teach new belayers on the ground, with an experienced belayer as a backup on the brake strand.

Most arborist climbing lines are 11 to 13 mm, outside the GriGri+ range, and tree climbing systems normally use purpose-built MRS or SRS devices. If you are considering it for any tree-work use, confirm compatibility with the rope and with Petzl's instructions first.

The GriGri is designed and certified as a belay device for rock and gym climbing. If you plan to use it in a tree-work system, make sure the configuration is covered by Petzl's instructions, that it meets ANSI Z133 requirements for life support, and that you are trained in it. Inspect it before every use.

Most tree crews will be better served by purpose-built devices for MRS and SRS, which are designed around arborist rope diameters and the way tree climbers move. The GriGri+ is a better fit for rock climbing and gym use.

Keep the device clean and dry, check the cam and anti-panic function before each session, and retire it if the rope channel shows deep wear or any part is cracked or bent. Record inspections for shared crew or gym gear.
Store it dry and away from chemicals that can damage the plastic. If the device has been dropped from height or caught a severe fall, inspect it carefully before using it again.

faq.q: Is the GriGri+ better than the GriGri?
faq.a: It adds anti-panic and a mode selector, which help new belayers and gyms. Experienced climbers often prefer the lighter standard GriGri.

faq.q: Which ropes work in the GriGri+?
faq.a: Single ropes from 8.5 to 11 mm.

faq.q: Does anti-panic make it hands-free?
faq.a: No. Always keep your brake hand on the rope.

name: Petzl Huit Figure 8 Descender
title: Petzl Huit Figure 8 Descender for Rope Work
meta: The Petzl Huit is a simple aluminum figure 8 descender for controlled rappels and lowering. How it works, where it fits for tree crews, and price.
tagline: Simple aluminum figure 8 descender for rappelling and lowering.
summary: The Petzl Huit is a classic figure 8 descender for controlled rappels and lowering. Its simple aluminum design is easy to rig, easy to inspect, and gives smooth friction on a range of single rope diameters.
highlights: Classic figure 8 shape
Aluminum body keeps weight low
Smooth, predictable friction
Easy to rig and inspect
Useful for rescue kits and training

p: The rope passes through the large eye and around the neck of the 8, creating friction as it slides. The user controls speed with a brake hand on the rope below the device. It is a simple tool with no moving parts, so there is little to go wrong and inspection takes seconds.
Climbing figure 8 descenders like the Huit are common in rescue, caving, and training kits because they rig quickly and work with gloves on.
The Huit is simple and inexpensive, so many crews keep one in the rescue bag. It does not need special rope or a complex setup, which can make a difference when every minute counts.

body.h: Where it fits for tree workers
p: Modern arborists usually descend on hitches, mechanical friction devices, or SRS devices designed for tree work. A figure 8 still has a place in a rescue kit for lowering or rappelling on a dedicated rescue line, and in training where students learn basic friction principles.

A figure 8 does not lock by itself. If you let go of the brake strand, it does not hold you. Anyone using it should be trained in tie-offs and have a backup where required. Compare devices built for tree work in our ascent and descent section.
Figure 8 descenders also have uses on the ground. For example, they can be used to add friction to a lowering line in light rigging, though dedicated rigging devices are better for regular use.
It is also a common first device for teaching how rope friction, wraps, and brake-hand position control speed on a descent.

Figure 8s are known for putting twist in a rope, especially on long descents. Keep the rope running straight into the device and shake out twists between uses. On long or fast lowers the aluminum can get hot enough to glaze nylon and polyester ropes, so control speed and let the device cool.
Pair the Huit with rope in the diameter range Petzl lists, and keep a locking carabiner dedicated to it.
For extra friction, the rope can be rigged in a different way through the device, but only use configurations shown in Petzl's instructions. Practice them on the ground before you need them.
Keep a dedicated rope for rescue, matched to the device, rather than relying on whatever climbing line happens to be on the truck.

Look for grooves worn by the rope, sharp edges, cracks, and corrosion. Retire it if a groove becomes deep or sharp enough to damage rope. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
Keep the Huit clean and dry. Wash it with fresh water if it has been exposed to salt or dirt, and let it dry before storage.

faq.q: Is a figure 8 descender auto-locking?
faq.a: No. The user must keep control of the brake strand at all times.

faq.q: Why does my rope twist after using a figure 8?
faq.a: The way the rope wraps the device induces twist. Feed the rope straight and shake out kinks regularly.

faq.q: Can I use a figure 8 for tree climbing?
faq.a: It is mainly a rescue and training tool for tree workers. For climbing, use devices designed and approved for arborist systems.

name: Petzl Ascension Hand Ascender
title: Petzl Ascender: Ascension Handled Rope Clamp
meta: The Petzl ascender most arborists know, the Ascension is a handled rope clamp for 8 to 13 mm single rope used on SRS ascents. Setup tips and typical price.
tagline: Handled rope clamp for SRS ascents on 8 to 13 mm rope.
summary: The Petzl Ascension is a handled ascender, the Petzl ascender most arborists picture when they think of a jumar. It grips single rope from 8 to 13 mm and is a staple of SRS ascent systems for climbing rope quickly into the canopy.
highlights: Ergonomic molded handle for gloved hands
Toothed cam grips rope from 8 to 13 mm
Top and bottom attachment holes
Available in left- and right-hand versions
Common part of SRS ascent systems

p: A hand ascender slides up the rope freely and locks when weighted downward. The toothed cam bites into the rope cover, so the clamp holds your weight while you move a foot ascender or a knee ascender up. A safety catch keeps the cam from opening accidentally.

On an arborist SRS ascent, the Ascension is typically paired with a foot ascender and a chest ascender or a hip-mounted device, or used in a rope walker or frog system. It is the hand-held link that lets you stand and push up efficiently.

The handle is shaped for gloved hands and a firm, comfortable grip during repeated strokes. The 8 to 13 mm rope range covers almost every arborist climbing line. Choose the hand version you will grip with: right-hand for most climbers, left-hand if you lead with your left.
Hand ascenders like this, sometimes called a jumar, are also used for rope rescue and tensioning systems. For fall protection, pair it with a device approved for life-support use within your system.

Many climbers choose the Ascension because it is one of the most widely used hand ascenders, so spare parts, accessories, and training resources are easy to find. The design has been refined over many years and is familiar to most trainers.

An ascender is for ascending, not for fall arrest. A shock load on a toothed cam can damage the rope sheath or the device. Keep slack out of the system, and do not climb above your ascender with a loose connection.

Ascend and descend only with a system you have been trained on. Your SRS should include a device that lets you descend and a way to transition safely. Pair it with a rope wrench or other SRS device for work positioning.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
Before you ascend, check that the cam is closed on the rope and the safety catch is engaged. Keep the ascender connected to your harness with a lanyard or tether so it cannot be dropped or lost.

Check the cam teeth for wear and packed sap or dirt, which reduce grip. Confirm the cam spring snaps closed, the safety catch works, and the frame is not cracked or bent. Clean with warm water and let it dry fully. Retire it if teeth are worn flat or the frame is damaged.
Store it dry and away from chemicals. If it has been dropped from height or loaded severely, inspect it carefully before using it again.
Keep the hand ascender clipped to your system when not in use. Losing it mid-ascent is a real hazard, and dropping it can injure someone on the ground.

faq.q: What rope does the Petzl Ascension fit?
faq.a: Single rope from 8 to 13 mm.

faq.q: Should I buy the right or left hand version?
faq.a: Choose the side you grip with. Most climbers use the right-hand version.

faq.q: Can a hand ascender catch a fall?
faq.a: No. It is for ascending. Fall protection must come from devices approved for that use.

name: Hitch Hiker 2 Mechanical Hitch Device
title: Hitch Hiker 2 Mechanical Friction Device for MRS
meta: The Hitch Hiker 2 is a mechanical device for doubled-rope (MRS) tree climbing that combines a hitch with a tending pulley. How it works, setup, and price.
tagline: Hitch-based mechanical device for smooth MRS climbing.
summary: The Hitch Hiker 2 is a mechanical friction device for doubled-rope (MRS) tree climbing that pairs a friction hitch with an integrated tending system. Climbers use the Hitch Hiker 2 to keep a smooth, slack-free system on long limb walks and quick ascents.
highlights: Designed for MRS hitch climbing
Integrated tending helps advance the hitch smoothly
Keeps slack out of the system
Familiar hitch feel with mechanical convenience
Second-generation design
specs: Mechanical friction device with hitch tender

p: The Hitch Hiker sits between your climbing line and your hitch, keeping the hitch in line with the rope and tending it as you move. You get the controlled release of a friction hitch with the smooth slack-tending of a pulley. It is aimed at climbers who like hitch climbing but want less fiddling, especially on long limb walks.

The second version refines the original design. Many climbers who searched for a hitch climber or hitch tender upgrade land here because it keeps a hitch-based system rather than switching fully to a mechanical device.
The device is compact and relatively light, which keeps your system tidy and close to your bridge. That helps on long limb walks where every bit of slack and extra hardware adds up.

Follow the manufacturer's instructions exactly for rope diameter, hitch cord, and which hitch to tie. Small changes in cord, wraps, or bridge setup change how the system grabs and releases. Set it up on the ground, test it with your full weight just off the ground, and adjust before you climb.
Pair it with a rope the device is approved for, such as an 11.7 mm line like Yale Poison Moon, and a properly sized bridge and carabiners.

Take your time with setup. A system that feels too grabby or too slippery usually needs small adjustments, such as a different number of wraps or a slightly different hitch cord. Make one change at a time and test it.

Fully mechanical devices like the Petzl Zigzag replace the hitch with a chain of metal links. The Hitch Hiker keeps a fiber hitch, which many climbers find more forgiving and familiar. Either way, your hitch cord is a wear item and should be replaced when glazed or stiff.
If you climb a lot of SRS, look at SRS devices instead; the Hitch Hiker is built around doubled-rope work.
Both systems take practice. If you are switching from a basic split-tail and pulley, plan a few climbs low in the tree to learn how the device behaves.
Check the device for cracks, sharp edges, and wear grooves, and inspect the hitch cord before every climb. Any change to the system should be tested low.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

Record when you put a new hitch cord into service and replace it on a schedule, not just when it looks worn. Hitch cords lose performance gradually, and a regular replacement schedule keeps the system predictable.
Store the device dry and away from chemicals, and keep it in a gear bag where it will not be knocked around by heavier tools.

faq.q: Is the Hitch Hiker 2 for MRS or SRS?
faq.a: It is designed for MRS, doubled-rope climbing.

faq.q: Which hitch cord should I use?
faq.a: Use the cord and hitch the manufacturer specifies for your rope diameter.

faq.q: Do I still need a micro pulley?
faq.a: The Hitch Hiker's tending function replaces a separate pulley in its system. Follow the instructions.

name: Petzl Zigzag Mechanical Friction Device
title: Petzl Zigzag Mechanical Prusik for Tree Climbing
meta: The Petzl Zigzag is a mechanical prusik for doubled-rope tree climbing on 11.5 to 13 mm rope. How it works, Zigzag vs Zigzag Plus, setup, and price.
tagline: Petzl's mechanical prusik for MRS tree climbing.
summary: The Petzl Zigzag is a mechanical prusik built for arborists climbing on a doubled rope (MRS). It replaces a friction hitch with a chain of metal links, giving precise control on descents and a consistent feel from first climb to last.
highlights: Mechanical prusik for MRS climbing
Chain of links gives smooth, precise friction
Integrated pulley tends slack
For 11.5 to 13 mm arborist ropes
No hitch cord to replace

p: Instead of a hitch, the Zigzag uses a chain of links that the rope weaves through. When you load it, the chain pinches the rope and holds you. Push the release handle and the friction eases so you can descend. An integrated pulley keeps the system tended as you advance the device, so slack never builds up.
Because the friction comes from metal links, not fiber, the feel stays the same as the device ages. There is no hitch cord to glaze or replace, and no changes when the cord gets wet or dirty.
The Zigzag is one of the best-known mechanical prusiks for tree climbing, and it is widely used by arborists across the world.
It also works well for long limb walks, where the integrated pulley keeps the system tight as you move out.

The Petzl Zigzag Plus adds a swivel at the attachment point, which helps keep the device aligned when you move around the tree and reduces rope twist. The standard Zigzag is a little lighter and simpler. Both work on the same 11.5 to 13 mm rope range and both are designed for doubled-rope work. The Zigzag can also be adapted for SRS with Petzl's chicane accessory, following Petzl's instructions.
Zigzag climbing has a short learning curve. Practice descending low in the tree until your release feels natural.
The device rewards a smooth hand. Squeeze the handle gently to start the descent, and use your other hand on the tail of the rope to control speed. Jerky movements make the descent uneven.

Pair the Zigzag with a rope in its listed range and with a smooth cover; 24-strand and kernmantle ropes are common choices. Use a locking connector between the Zigzag and your bridge, and a friction saver or ring setup at the anchor.

Clean the links regularly; sap and grit build up and change friction. Petzl publishes inspection steps and wear limits for the links and pulley. Compare it with the hitch-based Hitch Hiker 2 if you prefer a fiber hitch.

Climbers who switch from a friction hitch often note how consistent the Zigzag feels. That consistency helps on long workdays when you are tired and do not want to think about how the hitch is behaving.
Keep the device and rope clean; grit acts like sandpaper on the links and the rope cover.

Learn the Zigzag from a qualified instructor or under close supervision. Always test the device just off the ground before climbing. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
If the device has been dropped, loaded abnormally, or shows unusual wear, retire it. Store it dry and away from chemicals.

faq.q: What rope does the Petzl Zigzag work with?
faq.a: Ropes from 11.5 to 13 mm diameter, used in a doubled-rope system.

faq.q: Should I get the Zigzag or Zigzag Plus?
faq.a: The Plus adds a swivel that keeps the device aligned. The standard Zigzag is lighter and simpler.

faq.q: Can the Zigzag be used on SRS?
faq.a: With Petzl's chicane accessory and following Petzl's instructions, it can be configured for single-rope work.

name: ISC Rope Wrench
title: ISC Rope Wrench for SRS Tree Climbing
meta: The ISC Rope Wrench adds friction and tending to a hitch for SRS tree climbing. How the rope wrench works, tether options, setup, and typical price.
tagline: The device that made hitch-based SRS climbing practical.
summary: The ISC Rope Wrench is a friction device that sits above your hitch and turns a standard friction hitch into a practical single-rope (SRS) climbing system. The rope wrench adds the extra friction a hitch needs on a single line and keeps it tending smoothly as you move.
highlights: Adds friction above a hitch for SRS
Lets climbers keep a familiar hitch
Works with a flexible or rigid tether
Fits common arborist rope diameters
Proven design used widely in tree work
specs: SRS friction device (used with a hitch)
Friction hitch tied below the wrench

p: On a doubled rope, a friction hitch has the help of a 2:1 system. On a single stationary rope, a hitch alone usually grabs too hard to release smoothly or runs too fast to control. The ISC Rope Wrench solves that by bending the rope through a short channel above the hitch, adding friction there so the hitch only does part of the work.

The result is the hitch feel climbers know, on a stationary rope that can be anchored at the base or to a big canopy limb. It made SRS practical for many arborists before fully mechanical SRS devices were common.
The ISC Rope Wrench is one of the most widely used SRS friction devices in tree work, and many climbers learned SRS on it. ISC is a UK-based maker of climbing and rescue hardware.

The wrench connects to your hitch carabiner with a tether. A flexible tether lets the wrench move with the rope, while a rigid tether keeps it aligned and makes tending easier when you are not weighting the system. ISC sells the wrench with or without a tether; choose based on how you climb.

Use the hitch cord and hitch ISC recommends for your rope diameter, and tie the hitch below the wrench as shown in the instructions. A micro pulley below the hitch helps tend slack. Test the full system low before climbing.
Hitch choice matters. Many climbers use a Distel or VT hitch with the wrench. Too few wraps and the system slips; too many and it will not release. Adjust a little at a time and test.

SRS with a rope wrench shines on tall trees and big removals: you ascend quickly with a separate ascent system, then switch to the wrench for work positioning and descents. Pair it with a Petzl Ascension or other ascender for fast climbing.
Compared with fully mechanical SRS devices, a rope wrench system is lighter and familiar, but hitch cords wear and need regular replacement.

The rope wrench can also be used for work positioning on a base-tied line, which makes it easy to retrieve the rope from the ground after the job. Plan your anchor carefully, since forces on the anchor are different from MRS.

The rope rubs the wrench's wear surfaces, so check them for grooves, and replace wear parts according to ISC guidance. Inspect the tether, hitch cord, and carabiners every climb. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.
Clean sap and grit from the wrench regularly, and check the tether for wear, especially at connection points.
If you are new to SRS, have a qualified trainer check your setup and watch your first climbs.

faq.q: What does an ISC rope wrench do?
faq.a: It adds friction above a hitch so the hitch works smoothly on a single stationary rope.

faq.q: Do I need a tether?
faq.a: Yes. The wrench connects to your system with a flexible or rigid tether. ISC sells it with or without one.

faq.q: Can I use the rope wrench on MRS?
faq.a: It is designed for SRS. On a doubled rope a hitch alone usually gives enough friction.
